messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Nadia, a 38-year-old married woman from a Middle Eastern background, came to treatment after months of feeling as though her body had never really left the night she was assaulted. The event had happened when she was leaving a client’s apartment after a late cleaning shift. She remembered being cornered in a narrow hallway, someone shouting at her to stop struggling, and the humiliation of being forced to comply while she tried to protect herself. Even now, parts of that night remained painfully vivid to her: the angle of the hallway light, the harshness of the shouting, the pressure in her ribs and shoulders. Other moments were simply gone. She would say that she felt she was remembering only pieces, with whole stretches missing, and that the gaps were almost as disturbing as the fragments she could see so clearly. When the memory returned, she felt the same physical pain in the same parts of her body, as if her muscles were being dragged back into it.

In the weeks that followed, Nadia found that certain things outside could bring the whole experience rushing back. Being forced to do something, even in ordinary situations, struck her as especially dangerous because it echoed the loss of control she had felt during the assault. If a supervisor at work barked an order or a family member pressed her to agree before she was ready, she would feel her stomach tighten and her attention narrow. Shouting had the same effect. A raised voice from another room, a neighbor arguing in the hallway, even a loud television could make her freeze and feel suddenly unsafe. Reminders of victims, too—news stories, a woman looking frightened on the bus, or a client who seemed vulnerable and cornered—would pull her back toward the assault by making her think of how easily someone could be overpowered. These moments did not just upset Nadia; they made her body and mind shift into high alert, and she became convinced that danger could break in at any time.

As that fear took hold, Nadia began scanning constantly for signs of danger. At work as a housekeeper, she found herself checking every entrance before she settled into cleaning, listening for footsteps in the hallway, and watching the faces and voices of the people around her for any hint of anger. At home she would stop mid-task to listen for sounds that might mean someone was entering the apartment, especially when her husband was out or the children in the building were being loud in the corridor. Her concentration suffered because so much of her mind was spent tracking what might happen next. Even when she was scrubbing sinks or folding laundry, part of her remained fixed on the possibility of being surprised, trapped, or shouted at again. The more she scanned, the more ordinary encounters felt threatening, and the more any command, loud voice, or reminder of a frightened victim could set off the same surge of alarm. She had come to believe that staying alert was the only way to keep herself safe, yet it left her unable to relax long enough to feel present in her own day.

Over time, that constant vigilance began to shape how Nadia moved through the world. She started turning down extra jobs that involved late hours, avoided certain apartment buildings where she thought she might be boxed in, and found excuses to leave rooms when voices rose. These habits relieved her briefly, but they also kept her life shrinking around the fear. At work, she became slower and more distracted, needing to reread instructions and pausing often because her mind kept drifting back to watchfulness. At home, her husband noticed that she sat near the door and listened intently whenever someone passed in the stairwell. Nadia hated how easily she startled and how little room she had left in her head for anything else, but she felt that lowering her guard would be reckless. The assault had taught her, in the most concrete way possible, that being controlled, shouted at, or caught off guard could become unbearable in an instant.

What finally brought Nadia to seek help was that the strain was beginning to spill into every part of her marriage and work. She was afraid that if she kept living this way, she would lose her ability to function at all, and she was even more afraid that one loud voice in the wrong place would send her back into the same terror and pain. At the same time, she was hoping for something she had not allowed herself to imagine for months: to be able to move through her home, her job, and a simple conversation without constantly waiting for the next sign that something terrible was about to happen.
